objectives: Translate the statement “the rate of change depends on the current state and input” into a first-order differential equation, and explain why an initial condition is part of a complete prediction.
Derive the exact constant-input solution of \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I\) by hand and verify it using the initial value, long-time limit, and units.

prerequisiteBridge: Begin by reading \(dx/dt\) as “change in state divided by change in time” over a very short interval. A differential equation asks for an entire function \(x(t)\), not a single number: its slope at every time must obey the stated rule. A slope rule usually permits many shifted or scaled trajectories, so the state at one time, such as \(x(0)=x_{0}\), must also be specified. This is like starting from different points on the same road map: the route rule is unchanged, but later positions differ. Arrows in a phase portrait give local directions, and the initial condition chooses where motion along the flow begins.

The key property of \(e^{at}\) is that differentiation returns the same function times a constant: \(d(e^{at})/dt=a e^{at}\). It decays when \(a<0\) and grows when \(a>0\). A time constant \(\tau\) must carry units of time so that \(t/\tau\) is dimensionless. After one \(\tau\), a decaying exponential retains \(e^{-1}\approx 0.368\) of its initial value; after about \(3\tau\), it retains about 5%. This numerical intuition lets you judge the approach to steady state without relying on a plot.

A numerical simulation replaces a continuous trajectory with states at discrete times. Euler's method assumes that the current slope remains fixed throughout one step \(\Delta t\), so the next value equals the current value plus “step size × current slope.” A smaller step is usually more accurate but requires more calculations. A step that is too large can create oscillation or divergence absent from the continuous system. When reading code, keep four descriptions aligned: the continuous equation, the discrete update, parameter units, and boundary conditions. Compare at least two step sizes at the same physical time.

modules.title: From a rate of change to the exact solution of a first-order system
paragraphs: This section uses \(dx/dt=x\) and \(d^{2}x/dt^{2}=-x\) to show that a differential equation specifies a dynamical rule. A candidate solution is checked by substitution, not by visual resemblance. The derivative of \(x=e^t\) is \(e^t\), satisfying the first equation; the second derivative of \(x=\sin t\) is \(-\sin t\), satisfying the second. Initial conditions then select the amplitude and phase.

In \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I\), \(\tau\) is the response time constant and I is constant input. Write the right-hand side as −(x−I): the steady state is \(x^{*}=I\), with positive slope below I and negative slope above I. Let \(y=x-I\) be the deviation from steady state. The equation becomes \(\tau dy/dt=-y\), converting a constantly driven problem into pure exponential decay.

Separate variables to obtain \(dy/y=-dt/\tau\). Integration gives \(\ln|y|=-t/\tau +C\), and exponentiation gives \(y=Ae^{-t/\tau }\). Since \(y(0)=x_{0}-I\), \(A=x_{0}-I\) and \(x(t)=I+(x_{0}-I)e^{-t/\tau }\). The expression combines the steady state I with a fading memory of the initial condition; understanding those two terms matters more than memorizing the formula.

Apply three independent checks to the exact solution. Initial value: at \(t=0\) the exponential is 1, giving \(x_{0}\). Equation: differentiation gives \(\tau dx/dt=-(x_{0}-I)e^{-t/\tau }\), equal to −x+I. Long time: as \(t\to \infty\) the exponential vanishes and \(x\to I\). You can also verify the initial slope \((I-x_{0})/\tau\). Failure of any check rules out the candidate for this initial-value problem.
keyPoints: A differential equation determines a trajectory only when paired with an initial condition.
For constant input, the steady state is I and the deviation x−I decays exponentially.
The initial value, substitution into the equation, and the long-time limit provide three independent checks of the exact solution.

derivation.title: Step-by-step solution of a first-order linear system with constant input
derivation.setup: Solve \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I\) for \(x(0)=x_{0}\), assuming \(\tau >0\) and constant I.

steps.title: Find the steady state and shift variables
steps.explanation: Setting the derivative to zero gives \(x^{*}=I\). Define \(y=x-I\); because I is constant, \(dy/dt=dx/dt\).

steps.title: Separate variables
steps.explanation: Substitution gives \(\tau dy/dt=-y\). Wherever y is nonzero, rearrange to \(dy/y=-dt/\tau\); \(y=0\) itself is the steady-state solution.

steps.title: Integrate and exponentiate
steps.explanation: Integrating both sides gives \(\ln|y|=-t/\tau +C\). Absorb the sign into the constant to write \(y=A \exp(-t/\tau )\).

symbolNotes: \(x(t)\) is a time-varying state. In this derivation, I is simply a constant input and does not necessarily mean electrical current.
\(\tau >0\) determines the decay rate, and \(x_{0}\) is the state at \(t=0\).
derivation.unitsCheck: x, I, and \(x_{0}\) must have the same units. \(dx/dt\) has state/time units, multiplication by \(\tau\) restores state units, and \(t/\tau\) is dimensionless.
derivation.limitCheck: Smaller \(\tau\) produces more decay over the same t. If \(x_{0}=I\), the exponential coefficient is zero and the system remains at steady state from the start.

workedExample.title: Calculate a step response over several time constants
workedExample.problem: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\) and \(x_{0}=0\), with input held at \(I=5\) after \(t=0\). Calculate x at \(t=10 \mathrm{ms}\) and 30 ms, and find the first time x reaches 4.
workedExample.result: \(x(10 \mathrm{ms})\approx 3.16\), \(x(30 \mathrm{ms})\approx 4.75\), and x reaches 4 after approximately 16.1 ms.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The trajectory must rise monotonically from 0 without exceeding 5. All three results satisfy that condition, and reaching 80% of steady state takes about \(1.61\tau\).

pitfalls: Dropping the integration constant and thereby losing the ability to satisfy an arbitrary initial condition.
Treating \(\tau\) as a finite deadline at which steady state is reached; an exponential approaches its limit only asymptotically.

modules.title: Euler's method: from the derivative definition to a stable step size
paragraphs: The derivative definition gives \(dx/dt\approx [x(t+\Delta t)-x(t)]/\Delta t\). Substitute it into \(dx/dt=f(x,t)\) and evaluate the right-hand side at the current time to obtain forward Euler: \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}+\Delta t f(x_{n},t_{n})\). The method extends the current tangent by one step, so error arises because the true slope changes during that interval. Local error per step is usually of order \(\Delta t^{2}\); over a fixed total time, global error is of order \(\Delta t\).

For \(\tau dx/dt=-x+I\), Euler gives \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}+(\Delta t/\tau )(-x_{n}+I)\). Define \(\alpha =\Delta t/\tau\) and \(y_{n}=x_{n}-I\) to obtain \(y_{n+1}=(1-\alpha )y_{n}\). The continuous deviation always decays smoothly; the discrete deviation is controlled by amplification factor \(a=1-\alpha\). Its magnitude shrinks only when \(|a|<1\).

Solving \(|1-\alpha |<1\) gives \(0<\alpha <2\). For \(0<\alpha \le 1\), the deviation keeps its sign and approaches steady state monotonically. For \(1<\alpha <2\), it alternates sign while decaying. At \(\alpha =2\), its magnitude does not shrink; for \(\alpha >2\), it grows. This is a property of the algorithm, not the biology of the original differential equation. Choose the step size relative to the system's fastest time constant.

To verify a numerical implementation, compare the Euler trajectory with a known exact solution at the same times and repeat the calculation with \(\Delta t\) and \(\Delta t/2\). Roughly halving the error is consistent with a first-order method. Also check that the first array entry is the initial value, whether an update uses \(I_{n}\) or \(I_{n+1}\), and whether time and state arrays have matching lengths. These choices matter at segment boundaries.
keyPoints: An Euler step is the current state plus the step size times the current slope.
The stability interval for first-order decay is \(0<\Delta t/\tau <2\); the monotonic interval is narrower.
Doubling or halving the step size helps separate discretization error from model behavior.

derivation.title: Derive Euler stability from the amplification factor
derivation.setup: Apply forward Euler to no-input decay \(\tau dx/dt=-x\) and determine when every initial value converges to 0.

steps.title: Write the discrete update
steps.explanation: The derivative difference quotient gives \(x_{n+1}=x_{n}-(\Delta t/\tau )x_{n}\).

steps.title: Define the amplification factor
steps.explanation: Let \(a=1-\Delta t/\tau\). After n recursions, \(x_{n}=a^n x_{0}\).

steps.title: Require magnitude to decay
steps.explanation: For \(|x_{n}|\) to approach 0 for every finite \(x_{0}\), |a| must be less than 1.

steps.title: Solve the inequality
steps.explanation: Starting from \(-1<1-\Delta t/\tau <1\), subtract 1 and reverse signs to obtain \(0<\Delta t/\tau <2\).

symbolNotes: \(\Delta t\) is a numerical time step, not an intrinsic system parameter; \(\tau\) is the time constant of the continuous equation.
a is the dimensionless multiplier applied to the deviation on each step.
derivation.unitsCheck: \(\Delta t/\tau\) is dimensionless. Both terms added in the update have the same units as x.
derivation.limitCheck: As \(\Delta t\to 0\), \(a\to 1\): each change is small but the number of steps grows. At \(\Delta t=\tau\), \(a=0\) and the no-input discrete solution reaches zero in one step; that does not reproduce the intermediate continuous exponential.

workedExample.title: First four states at three step sizes
workedExample.problem: Let \(\tau =10 \mathrm{ms}\), \(I=0\), and \(x_{0}=1\). For \(\Delta t=5\), 15, and 25 ms, calculate the first three updates and classify the behavior.
steps: For \(\Delta t=5\), \(a=0.5\) and the sequence is 1, 0.5, 0.25, 0.125: monotonic decay.
For \(\Delta t=15\), \(a=-0.5\) and the sequence is 1, −0.5, 0.25, −0.125: alternating decay.
For \(\Delta t=25\), \(a=-1.5\) and the sequence is 1, −1.5, 2.25, −3.375: divergent magnitude.
The continuous system is the same positive exponential decay in all three cases; every difference comes from the numerical step size.
workedExample.result: 5 ms gives stable monotonic decay, 15 ms gives stable oscillatory decay, and 25 ms gives unstable divergence.
workedExample.sanityCheck: The three amplification-factor magnitudes are 0.5, 0.5, and 1.5, matching the observed decrease, decrease, and increase in magnitude.

pitfalls: Accepting a trajectory because the program ran without error, without checking \(\Delta t\) relative to \(\tau\).
Changing total duration or input sampling together with step size, making the error comparison uninterpretable.

modules.title: Second-order oscillator, state space, and code-boundary audit
paragraphs: The second-order equation \(d^{2}x/dt^{2}=-x\) needs both position x and velocity \(v=dx/dt\) to determine the future. Defining v gives \(dx/dt=v\) and \(dv/dt=-x\), so state \(z=(x,v)^{\mathrm{T}}\) evolves in a two-dimensional plane. For the continuous system, \(E=(x^{2}+v^{2})/2\) has derivative \(x\cdot dx/dt+v\cdot dv/dt=xv-vx=0\). The trajectory is therefore a closed curve of fixed radius, not an inward or outward spiral.

A physical oscillator must retain angular frequency \(\omega\). Under forward Euler, an energy-like quantity is multiplied by \(1+(\omega \Delta t)^{2}\) on every step. No finite \(\Delta t\) conserves it exactly, so a long simulation drifts outward. This does not mean Euler fails to converge: with total duration fixed and \(\Delta t\to 0\), cumulative amplification approaches 1 and the numerical trajectory approaches the continuous solution. Only after setting \(\omega =1\) and nondimensionalizing time can the factor be shortened to \(1+\Delta t^{2}\) as in the notes.

The accompanying code also simulates a first-order system with \(\tau =0.01 \mathrm{s}\), step 0.001 s, and duration 0.250 s. Inputs are 0, 2, 1, a cosine, and 0 in sequence. Each update reads the previous input \(I(t-1)\), as expected for the current-time slope in explicit Euler. The final condition is `time<0.250`, but the time vector includes the endpoint 0.250 exactly. Consequently, \(I(end)\) remains NaN and the last input point is not plotted normally.

That NaN does not immediately contaminate \(x(end)\), because the final state update reads \(I(end-1)\), not \(I(end)\). This demonstrates why “the output looks normal” does not prove that an array is complete. A second semantic error concerns \(t_{0}=0.150\) in \(\cos(\omega (t-t_{0}))\): this is a phase-reference time, so a comment calling it a frequency conflicts with its units. The actual frequency parameter is angular frequency \(\omega =220 \mathrm{rad}/s\). Audit comments, formulas, units, and indices together.
keyPoints: A second-order system can be represented by two coupled first-order equations for position and velocity.
Forward Euler multiplies an undamped oscillator's energy-like quantity by \(1+(\omega \Delta t)^{2}\) each step; only the nondimensional \(\omega =1\) form becomes \(1+\Delta t^{2}\).
Array endpoints, strict inequalities, and use of a previous index jointly determine whether NaN propagates.

derivation.title: Prove the finite-step energy drift of forward Euler
derivation.setup: Apply step h to \(dx/dt=v\) and \(dv/dt=-\omega ^{2}x\). Define twice the energy-like quantity as \(2E=v^{2}+\omega ^{2}x^{2}\) and compare E before and after one Euler step.

steps.title: Write both updates
steps.explanation: Advance position along the current velocity and change velocity along the current restoring acceleration.

steps.title: Expand the updated energy
steps.explanation: Expand \(v_{n+1}^{2}\) and \(\omega ^{2}x_{n+1}^{2}\) separately; their cross terms have equal magnitude and opposite sign.

steps.title: Cancel the cross terms
steps.explanation: Adding the expansions leaves the original energy multiplied by a factor strictly greater than 1.

steps.title: Accumulate the finite-step error
steps.explanation: With total duration \(T=nh\), the energy ratio after n repetitions is the expression below. Every fixed \(h>0\) produces outward drift.

steps.title: Check the convergence limit
steps.explanation: At fixed T, let \(h\to 0\). The logarithm of the ratio is approximately \(T\omega ^{2}h\) and approaches 0, so the energy ratio approaches 1. Euler is not conservative, but it still converges on a finite time interval.

symbolNotes: \(\omega\) is angular frequency with units of inverse time. The notes' \(dv/dt=-x\) corresponds to \(\omega =1\) in nondimensional time.
h is the numerical step and T is the fixed total duration used for comparison. A statement about energy drift must specify both.
derivation.unitsCheck: hv has the same units as x, \(h\omega ^{2}x\) has the same units as v, and \(\omega h\) is dimensionless. Because \(v^{2}\) and \(\omega ^{2}x^{2}\) share units, they can form one energy-like quantity.
derivation.limitCheck: For every finite \(h>0\), the per-step factor exceeds 1. At fixed T with \(h\to 0\), the cumulative factor approaches 1. If T grows as 1/h or faster, long-time structural error may remain substantial.

workedExample.title: Locate an endpoint bug in a piecewise input
workedExample.problem: The time vector is 0:0.001:0.250. The last input branch assigns 0 only when \(t<0.250\); all other values remain preallocated as NaN. How many time points exist, which one is NaN, and does it enter the final x update?
steps: From 0 to 0.250 in increments of 0.001 gives \(0.250/0.001+1=251\) points.
The final point \(t=0.250\) fails the strict inequality \(t<0.250\), so \(I(251)\) remains NaN.
If the loop computes \(x(k)\) from \(I(k-1)\), then \(x(251)\) reads \(I(250)\), which corresponds to \(t=0.249\) and equals 0.
Thus \(x(251)\) remains finite in the current loop, but the input plot lacks its last point. Any later read of \(I(251)\) would propagate NaN.
workedExample.result: There are 251 points, and \(I(251)\) is NaN. It does not enter the final explicit update here, but it exposes a gap in the boundary conditions.
workedExample.sanityCheck: An interval of length 0.250 s contains 250 steps of this size, so it must contain 1 more endpoint than steps.

pitfalls: Interpreting a spiral in a phase portrait as damping or self-excitation before checking the discrete update matrix.
Trusting variable comments without checking how the variable appears in equations and what units it carries.
Missing the final array assignment because the time vector includes the right endpoint while the branch uses a strict inequality.

figures.title: Exact exponential decay versus Euler approximation
figures.alt: Comparison of the exact solution of first-order exponential decay with Euler points using a step equal to half the time constant
figures.caption: For \(\tau dx/dt=-x\), forward Euler advances one step along the current tangent. With \(\Delta t=\tau /2\) it is stable, but at finite step size it decays faster than the exact exponential. Reducing \(\Delta t\) moves the discrete points toward the exact curve.
